subject: Biology
title: Pack Hunting: Wolves and Orcas
description: A micro-lesson that makes Pack Hunting: Wolves and Orcas usable.

hook.text: A lone wolf can take a rabbit. A pack of wolves can take down a bison ten times their size.

buildup.text: Pack hunting requires coordination, communication, and role specialization.

discovery.text: Orcas use coordinated waves to wash seals off ice floes—a tactic taught from parent to calf.

twist.text: African wild dogs vote on hunts by sneezing. More sneezes mean higher commitment to go.

climax.text: Social hunters share food, increasing survival for the group even when individuals miss a meal.

punchline.text: Hunt alone, eat small. Hunt together, eat big.

quiz.question: How do African wild dogs vote on whether to hunt?

details.summary: Pack hunting involves coordinated group strategies to capture prey that individuals could not take alone. Wolves use relay chasing and strategic positioning, while orcas create waves to wash seals off ice floes, demonstrating learned cultural hunting techniques.
details.whyItMatters: Cooperative hunting reveals social intelligence, communication, and role specialization in animal groups. It shows how cooperation can create capabilities far beyond what any individual possesses.
takeaways: Wolves coordinate roles like drivers and ambushers during hunts
Orca hunting techniques are culturally transmitted within pods
Pack hunting enables predators to take prey much larger than themselves

faq.question: How do wolves coordinate their hunting strategies?
faq.answer: Wolves communicate through body language, vocalizations, and positioning. Experienced pack members take specific roles based on the terrain and prey. Some chase the target toward waiting ambushers, requiring anticipation of prey movement.

faq.question: Do pack hunters share food equally?
faq.answer: Rarely. In wolf packs, dominant individuals eat first. However, the benefits of group hunting still outweigh solo hunting for all members because cooperative strategies access prey that no individual could kill alone.
